articles.title: The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change
articles.summary: The global campaign to restore the "soggy secret weapon" that can combat against climate change.
articles.content:
Most people know rainforests are vital in the fight against climate change, but now scientists say wetlands could be even more important.

Saltmarshes, mangrove swamps and wetlands can absorb carbon "four times faster than trees", according to the charity the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT).

Celebrating 80 years since WWT's first wetland bird reserve was founded at Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, the charity's leaders have called for one million hectares of wetlands to be restored across the world.

Sarah Fowler, CEO of WWT, said: "They are mood-boosting, flood-buffering, water-purifying, incredible habitats. But we have lost 85% of the world's wetlands."
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the significant role of wetlands in combating climate change by absorbing carbon faster than trees. It reports on a global campaign to restore one million hectares of wetlands, which has broad environmental benefits and addresses a major issue of wetland loss worldwide. The story is focused, detailed, and presents a meaningful positive environmental impact.
articles.personality_title: Wetlands: Nature’s fast carbon absorbers in the fight against climate change
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Wetlands like saltmarshes, mangrove swamps, and marshes are natural areas that hold water and support many plants and animals. While rainforests are well-known for helping fight climate change, scientists have found wetlands might be even better at removing harmful carbon from the air.

**What happened** – The Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT), a charity celebrating 80 years of protecting wetland birds, shared new research showing wetlands absorb carbon four times faster than trees. To help the planet, WWT is leading a campaign to restore one million hectares of wetlands worldwide.

**Impact** – This is important because wetlands do more than absorb carbon. They also help clean water, reduce flooding, and provide homes for wildlife. Sadly, 85% of the world's wetlands have been lost, so restoring them can bring back these benefits and slow climate change faster.

**What's next step** – The WWT and its partners will work with communities and governments to bring back wetlands. This effort includes planting new plants, protecting existing wetlands, and raising awareness about their value.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Restoring wetlands, which absorb carbon faster than trees and provide many environmental benefits, is a key step in fighting climate change and protecting nature.

articles.title: House martin artificial nests scheme set to expand
articles.summary: The artificial nests are more robust than the endangered migratory birds' own mud creations.
articles.content:
Up to 900 artificial nest "cups" for threatened house martins are set to be installed in Hampshire as part of a conservation project.

The birds migrate from Africa each spring and are on the UK's Red List of endangered bird species. They are thought to have suffered from a lack of wet mud to build nests during the extreme heat in the summer.

Following a pilot project, The Hampshire House Martins Project is offering free cups which save the birds time and energy compared to building their own mud nests.

Project co-ordinator Nigel Matthews encouraged residents, schools and businesses to apply for the free artificial nests "to give these remarkable birds a safe place to raise their young".

Between 1995 and 2024, the UK House Martin population fell by 40%, partly due to poor breeding success.

The birds build distinctive cup-shaped nests beneath the roofs of houses and other buildings, carrying around 1,000 pellets of soft mud to complete each one.

Each April and May, house martins return from Africa to spend the summer in the UK.

The birds often form colonies with several nests in close proximity.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a conservation project providing artificial nests to support the endangered house martin bird population, which has declined significantly. This initiative has a broad environmental impact by aiding a threatened species, involves community participation, and addresses a specific ecological challenge with clear, detailed context.

**Impact** – This project supports a bird species on the UK’s Red List of endangered birds. By providing ready-made nests, it helps the birds raise their young more easily, which could improve their chances of survival. It also involves local communities in protecting wildlife.

**What’s next step** – More artificial nests will be installed across Hampshire, and the project encourages more people to apply for free nests. If successful, the idea might spread to other areas to help house martins recover.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Free artificial nests in Hampshire give endangered house martins a safer and easier way to raise their young, helping their population to grow again.

articles.title: How microbes can secure the critical minerals the world needs
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03629-4To sustain supplies of key metals, policymakers should support the infrastructure needed to deploy mining biotechnologies on a large scale.
articles.content:
Copper compounds (blue) can be extracted from solution using microorganisms — a process known as bioleaching. Credit: Dirk Wiersma/Science Photo Library

The clean-energy transition is creating a paradox. To expand renewable-energy technologies, electrify transport and build infrastructure for artificial intelligence, society must extract unprecedented quantities of minerals. Demand for many of these ‘critical minerals’ is projected to increase several-fold over the coming decades1. Yet, the technologies used to obtain them remain rooted in an old model through which single metals are extracted from virgin ore2.

The consequences are increasingly apparent (see ‘Critical-mineral supply under pressure’). As deposits of high-grade ores decline, larger quantities of rock must be mined and processed to produce the same amount of metal3. That requires more energy and water. Mining accounts for around 1.7% of global energy consumption and this number is projected to rise by up to eight-fold by 20604. Many critical-mineral projects operate in regions facing high water stress, such as arid parts of Africa and Latin America1.

Sources: Top to bottom: Ref. 3; ref. 3; ref. 6 and go.nature.com/4nzbbnx

Mining waste is growing, too. Already, hundreds of billions of tonnes of mine tailings are stored globally. Projections suggest that by 2050, up to two trillion tonnes of extra waste rock and tailings will have accumulated3,5.

Meanwhile, society is producing vast quantities of metal-rich waste that remain a mostly untapped secondary source of metals. In 2022, 62 million tonnes of electronic waste (e-waste) was produced globally — almost 8 kilograms for every person on the planet — and only around 22% of that was formally collected and recycled6.

How to widen access to the critical minerals that the world needs

Many discarded electronics contain valuable metals, including gold, palladium and rare-earth elements — in concentrations that can exceed those found in primary ores. However, recovering these metals remains technically challenging and is often economically unattractive using conventional approaches.

Retrieval of metals and increasing metal circularity should be seen as a strategic capability to offset the growth of metal extraction from virgin ores. Nations that can efficiently recover critical minerals from waste streams, mine residues and low-grade resources will be less exposed to geopolitical disruptions and supply-chain shocks7.

Biology offers a powerful route forwards. Although biomining — which uses microorganisms to extract metals — was once considered a niche approach, it has evolved. Driven by advances in microbial ecology, synthetic biology, structural biology, protein engineering and machine learning, the scientific foundations for a new generation of mineral biotechnologies are emerging at speed8,9. These methods offer potential levels of selectivity for extracting and recovering certain metals that are often difficult to achieve through conventional hydrometallurgical processes.

But, scientific progress alone will not transform mineral supply chains. The main obstacle is no longer a shortage of ideas. It is a lack of pathways from scientific discovery to industrial deployment. Here we outline how to develop those pathways, drawing on discussions at the International Workshop on Biomining of Critical Minerals and Elements, which was sponsored by the Novo Nordisk Foundation and held in Sitges, Spain, in September last year.

Promising technologies

Biotechnologies have demonstrated their industrial potential for decades. Bioleaching and biooxidation processes are already established for recovering copper, nickel, gold and cobalt from ores10. They involve irrigating heaps of crushed ore or treating ground mineral powders with specialist microbes that generate chemicals, such as acids or modifiers of reduction–oxidation reactions, that selectively dissolve either target metals or other minerals found with them.

Advances in synthetic biology have expanded the range of potential applications. For example, engineered microbial systems can be designed to dissolve metals more effectively. Biomolecules (such as the protein lanmodulin) can separate rare-earth elements with yields of 99.9% in one step under conditions that are simpler than conventional techniques, using aqueous solutions rather than organic solvents8,11. AI-assisted protein design is further accelerating the discovery of macromolecules designed to selectively recognize, bind to and separate target metals from complex solutions of several elements9.

How the rush for critical minerals is neglecting human needs

Collectively, these developments suggest that biotechnology could become an important component of future critical-mineral supply chains. However, many promising approaches never progress beyond being validated in the laboratory. They often stall between proof-of-concept studies and commercial demonstration, a challenge familiar throughout industrial biotechnology. Even promising technologies often struggle to attract the capital, infrastructure and industrial partnerships needed to scale them up12,13.

Barriers must be overcome. Although a few bioprocessing pilot projects exist, their capacity is insufficient to evaluate technologies across the diverse types of ore, feedstock and process conditions encountered in practice. Investors are reluctant to finance first-of-a-kind projects when it is uncertain how well they will perform in the real world.

Regulatory frameworks for emerging biomining technologies are also inadequate. They often vary across biotechnology, environmental and mining sectors and between jurisdictions. Developers might need to navigate several regulatory authorities and approval pathways, creating uncertainty and delays as technologies advance.

Electronic waste can contain higher concentrations of key metals than are found in natural ores.Credit: Martin Bernetti/AFP via Getty

In the European Union, for example, the use of genetically modified microorganisms and their environmental applications are subject to distinct regulatory frameworks. Genetically modified microorganisms are allowed to be used in contained systems, whereas those used for field applications generally rely on naturally occurring or adapted microbial strains. The United States uses a coordinated multi-agency approach, involving the Environmental Protection Agency, the Food and Drug Administration and the US Department of Agriculture.

Valuable technical knowledge (on protein engineering, mineral characterization, hydrometallurgy and economic modelling, for instance) remains dispersed across disciplines, institutions and jurisdictions. This makes it difficult to generate the necessary evidence base — including long-term continuous operating data, metrics for tracking chemical cycles and validated economic assessments — to support large-scale adoption of such technologies.

The result is a growing mismatch. Scientific advances in mineral biotechnology are accelerating, yet the mechanisms needed to deploy them are not keeping pace. Although billions of dollars are being invested to secure future supply chains for critical minerals, comparatively little attention has been devoted to building the innovation systems required to commercialize biological solutions.

If biotechnology is to contribute meaningfully to critical-mineral security, environmental sustainability and circularity of resource use, then governments, industry, development banks and philanthropic funders must move beyond supporting research alone. They must invest in the institutions that enable translation of these new technologies as well.

Three priorities deserve attention.

Establish test facilities

Countries should establish shared pilot and demonstration facilities dedicated to mineral biotechnology. Individual companies often cannot justify the risks associated with developing specialized infrastructure for technologies that remain commercially unproven. Shared facilities can help to overcome this barrier by allowing several organizations to evaluate biological processes using realistic feedstocks under industrially relevant conditions. These facilities can support both pre-commercial and competitive studies. Similar approaches have been implemented successfully in synthetic biology and bio-refining, advanced manufacturing and in the clean-energy and semiconductor sectors.

The dark side of green technology: what do electric vehicles really cost?

For the mineral sector, such facilities should be located near relevant resource and waste streams, including mining districts, e-waste recycling hubs and sites affected by acid mine drainage or metal-laden urban waste waters. They should have connections to universities, research labs and a skilled workforce.

Access to research and engineering expertise would enable rapid iteration, troubleshooting and integration of mineral biotechnologies with established processes. Such sites would extend beyond technology testing to generate the operational, environmental and economic data needed to inform investment decisions, regulatory approvals and commercial deployment.

Initiatives in other sectors illustrates the value of such infrastructure. In Sweden, for instance, publicly funded pilot and demonstration facilities have been set up to test processes for biochemically converting biomass under realistic conditions14.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights significant scientific advances in biomining technologies that can sustainably secure critical minerals essential for clean energy and technology infrastructure, addressing environmental and resource challenges on a broad scale. It discusses the potential large-scale benefits of biotechnology in reducing mining waste, energy consumption, and reliance on virgin ores, with detailed context on current challenges and proposed solutions, making it a substantive and impactful positive development.
articles.personality_title: Microbes offer a new way to safely get the minerals we need
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**
The world needs more minerals like copper, gold, and rare earth elements to build clean energy, electric cars, and smart technology. But mining these minerals the usual way uses a lot of energy and water, creates huge waste, and is getting harder as good-quality ores run out.

**What happened**
Scientists are developing new methods that use tiny living things called microbes to extract metals from ores and waste. This process is called biomining. It is already used for some metals like copper and gold, but new advances in biology and artificial intelligence are making it possible to recover even rare and tricky metals more efficiently and with less harm to the environment.

**Impact**
Biomining can help reduce the amount of rock mined and the waste produced. It can also recover valuable metals from electronic waste, which often has more metal than natural ores. This means fewer resources are wasted, and mining can be done in a cleaner, more sustainable way. However, many promising biomining technologies are still stuck in labs because they need bigger testing facilities and clearer rules to be used widely.

**What's next step**
Experts suggest building shared pilot centers where companies and researchers can test biomining methods on a larger scale using real mining waste and electronic scrap. These centers would speed up improvements, help create jobs, and provide important data for investors and regulators. Governments and industries need to invest in these facilities and create clear regulations to make biomining a common tool for mining critical minerals.

**One-sentence takeaway**
Using microbes to mine metals offers a cleaner, smarter way to meet our growing mineral needs, but it needs support to move from labs to real-world use.

articles.title: Electric ferries that fly above water are arriving in the US
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Water has always been part of how many American cities move people, but for most of the country’s history it has been an afterthought compared to roads and rails. A new generation of electric ferries is beginning to change that, and some of them work in a way that […]
The post Electric ferries that fly above water are arriving in the US first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Water has always been part of how many American cities move people, but for most of the country’s history it has been an afterthought compared to roads and rails. A new generation of electric ferries is beginning to change that, and some of them work in a way that is surprising: they handle the problem of water by getting out of it.

The physics problem that held electric boats back

Electrifying boats has always been harder than electrifying cars, and the reason comes down to drag. Water resists a moving vessel far more than air resists a moving vehicle, which means boats require substantially more energy per mile. That high energy demand, combined with the weight of batteries, has made it difficult to design an electric vessel that can carry enough passengers far enough to be useful as everyday transit.

Hydrofoils get around this in a way that seems almost too obvious once you hear it. These vessels use underwater wings to lift the hull clear of the water as they accelerate, and once the hull is airborne, drag drops sharply. Vessev, a company that builds fully electric hydrofoil boats, says its design cuts drag by about 66 percent, which lets the boats carry smaller, lighter battery packs without sacrificing range. “We substantially reduce the drag that you feel, and that’s really what makes electrification viable,” said Eric Laakmann, Vessev’s chief executive and co-founder.

What the ride is like

The transition happens fast. As a Vessev boat accelerates through New York Harbor, the hydrofoils push the hull about a foot and a half above the surface, and the sensation of a boat working against waves gives way almost immediately to something smoother and quieter, closer to gliding than crossing water. “We’re picking up speed. We’re going for a takeoff,” Laakmann said during a recent demonstration, drawing curious looks from passengers on a nearby sightseeing ferry. His company is still a novelty to most people on the water, and he knows it.

From demonstration to daily commute

Vessev operates passenger services in New Zealand, with Australia next and its first US route planned for Lake Tahoe. Laakmann’s ambition runs past tourism: he wants electric vessels to be as unremarkable as buses, something commuters use because it’s there. “More like subways, more like buses, more like Ubers, more like taxis but on the water,” he said.

That idea has already taken root in parts of Europe. Stockholm commuters are riding electric hydrofoil ferries built by the Swedish company Candela, which says its design uses as much as 80 percent less energy than conventional vessels of a similar type. Norway has ordered 20 of the same boats for coastal service. The US is later to this shift, but several cities are starting to move.

San Francisco prepares for a half-billion-dollar overhaul

San Francisco carries about 3.5 million ferry passengers a year across a region shaped by its bay, and every one of the 18 vessels in the current fleet runs on diesel. Four battery-powered ferries are set to join the fleet over the next two years as part of an electric overhaul worth roughly half a billion dollars, including new charging infrastructure at its docks.

Converting a ferry network is more complicated than swapping out a car fleet. Ferries run on fixed schedules and cannot stop mid-route to recharge, so operators have to design the entire system around the relationship between battery range, trip time, and how much power the shoreside chargers can deliver in the minutes a vessel sits at the terminal. Seamus Murphy, who runs the agency, put it plainly: “We have a lot of waterfront.” San Francisco’s new vessels won’t use hydrofoil technology, but the agency says they’ll make it the first ferry operator in the country to run high-speed, all-electric service.

The economics of a fleet switch

For a long time, the financial math and the environmental math didn’t add up at the same time. Battery-powered ferries cost more upfront, but electric motors tend to be more efficient than diesel engines, and the savings on fuel and maintenance accumulate. Rising diesel costs have shifted the balance, as has continued progress in battery technology.

“You make the upfront investment at the beginning and then you save over time, and at the end of the day you’re going to have lower costs in the long term,” Murphy said. How well that holds up depends on the route: long distances, tight turnaround windows, and limited charging opportunities can all make the switch impractical. Not every waterway is suited to a fully electric vessel. For shorter commuter routes in cities with the right geography, though, the numbers are starting to work.

For San Francisco’s expansion, both the boats and their batteries are being manufactured in the US. Murphy sees this as a window that won’t stay open indefinitely. “These jobs are going to get created in other countries and we have an ability to create them here if we manage this in the right way,” he said. “We don’t want to be left behind.”

Water as working transit

Transportation is the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the US, and watercraft burning diesel contribute their share, particularly around busy ports and waterfront neighborhoods. Electric ferries could cut both emissions and the localized air pollution that diesel docks generate, while also opening up routes that weren’t previously viable and connecting communities by water without the cost of new roads or rail.

It won’t happen all at once. Some cities will move fast; others will take years to follow. But the direction looks clear. “I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Laakmann said, standing on a boat that had just crossed a harbor without burning a drop of fuel.

articles.personality_title: Electric hydrofoil ferries bring cleaner, faster water travel to US cities
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For many years, American cities have mainly focused on roads and trains to move people, while water travel was less common. Boats have been harder to make electric because water creates a lot of resistance, which uses more energy than cars need.

**What happened** – A new type of electric ferry that uses underwater wings called hydrofoils is arriving in the US. These hydrofoils lift the boat above the water, reducing drag by about two-thirds. This technology lets the boats use smaller batteries and travel farther without using much energy. Companies like Vessev plan to start services in places like Lake Tahoe, while cities like San Francisco are adding electric ferries to their fleets.

**Impact** – These electric hydrofoil ferries are quieter, smoother, and cleaner than traditional diesel boats. They cut pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, especially near busy waterfronts. San Francisco’s planned upgrade, including new charging docks, will make it the first US city with fast, all-electric ferry service. This shift also creates new jobs in the US for building these boats and batteries.

**What’s next step** – More cities with waterways are likely to add electric ferries as battery technology improves and costs go down. Operators must carefully plan routes and charging times to make the system work well. Meanwhile, companies will continue expanding services and exploring new places where electric boats can replace diesel ones.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Electric hydrofoil ferries are starting to transform water travel in the US by offering a cleaner, faster, and more energy-efficient way to move people across cities.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les ferries hydrofoils électriques apportent un transport maritime plus propre et rapide aux villes américaines
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Pendant longtemps, les villes américaines ont surtout utilisé les routes et les trains pour déplacer les gens, l’eau étant moins exploitée. Les bateaux électriques ont été difficiles à développer car l’eau oppose une forte résistance, ce qui demande beaucoup d’énergie.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Un nouveau type de ferry électrique équipé d’ailes sous-marines appelées hydrofoils arrive aux États-Unis. Ces hydrofoils soulèvent la coque hors de l’eau, réduisant la résistance d’environ deux tiers. Cette technologie permet d’utiliser des batteries plus petites et d’étendre l’autonomie sans trop consommer. Des entreprises comme Vessev prévoient de lancer des services au lac Tahoe, tandis que San Francisco prépare l’arrivée de ferries électriques.

**Impact** – Ces ferries électriques sont plus silencieux, plus confortables et plus propres que les bateaux diesel traditionnels. Ils réduisent la pollution et les émissions de gaz à effet de serre, notamment près des quais très fréquentés. La modernisation de San Francisco, avec de nouvelles bornes de recharge, en fera la première ville américaine à proposer un service de ferry rapide et entièrement électrique. Les opérateurs devront bien planifier les itinéraires et les temps de recharge pour que le système fonctionne efficacement. Pendant ce temps, les entreprises continueront à étendre leurs services et à explorer de nouveaux endroits.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Les ferries hydrofoils électriques commencent à transformer le transport maritime aux États-Unis en offrant une manière plus propre, plus rapide et plus économe en énergie de déplacer les personnes en ville.
articles.personality_title_es: Los ferris hidroala eléctricos traen un transporte acuático más limpio y rápido a las ciudades de EE.UU.
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante mucho tiempo, las ciudades estadounidenses han usado principalmente carreteras y trenes para mover a las personas, mientras que el transporte por agua era menos común. Los barcos eléctricos han sido difíciles de desarrollar porque el agua ofrece mucha resistencia, lo que requiere más energía.

**Qué pasó** – Un nuevo tipo de ferry eléctrico que usa alas bajo el agua llamadas hidroalas está llegando a EE.UU. Estas hidroalas levantan el casco del barco fuera del agua, reduciendo la resistencia en aproximadamente dos tercios. Esta tecnología permite usar baterías más pequeñas y viajar más lejos con menos energía. Empresas como Vessev planean iniciar servicios en lugares como el lago Tahoe, mientras que ciudades como San Francisco están agregando ferris eléctricos a sus flotas.

**Impacto** – Estos ferris eléctricos son más silenciosos, suaves y limpios que los barcos diésel tradicionales. Reducen la contaminación y las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero, especialmente cerca de los muelles concurridos. La actualización planeada de San Francisco, que incluye nuevos puntos de carga, la convertirá en la primera ciudad de EE.UU. con servicio rápido de ferry totalmente eléctrico. Este cambio también crea nuevos empleos en EE.UU. para construir estos barcos y baterías.

**Próximo paso** – Más ciudades con vías navegables probablemente añadirán ferris eléctricos a medida que la tecnología de baterías mejore y los costos bajen. Los operadores deben planificar cuidadosamente las rutas y los tiempos de carga para que el sistema funcione bien. Mientras tanto, las empresas seguirán expandiendo servicios y explorando nuevos lugares donde los barcos eléctricos puedan reemplazar a los diésel.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los ferris hidroala eléctricos están comenzando a transformar el transporte por agua en EE.UU. al ofrecer una forma más limpia, rápida y eficiente de mover personas en las ciudades.
